On Friday evening Julien takes Ioana to a “bouchon”, Lyon’s traditional restaurant. Karim comes too.
Good evening! Three of you? Here’s the menu.
Thank you. Ioana, here we eat Lyon cuisine.
I’m having the set menu: a Lyon salad, then quenelles.
I don’t eat meat. Do you have fish?
Yes, we have salmon with vegetables.
And I’d like the dish of the day, please.
A bottle of red wine and a jug of water, please.
A jug of water? Is it free?
Yes! In France, tap water is free in restaurants.
Yes, a praline tart! And three coffees, please.
IEN is read as a nasal “yẽ”: bien = “byẽ”, italien = “ee-ta-LYẼ”. In the feminine, “ienne” loses the nasal: italienne = “ee-ta-LYEN”.
L’eau = “lo”, like the letter o. Careful: “l’eau” (water) and “l’os” (bone) sound almost the same; context decides.
S between two vowels is read “z”: poison = “pwa-ZÕ” (poison!), but poisson, with SS, = “pwa-SÕ” (fish). Don’t mix them up in a restaurant!
Ç (c with a cedilla) is always read “s”: ça = “sa”, garçon = “gar-SÕ”, français = “frahn-SEH”.
The verb BOIRE: je bois = “zhuh BWA”, nous buvons = “noo bu-VÕ”. The “buv-” forms have the French U, with rounded lips.
1. Politeness in a restaurant: je voudrais, je prends
To order, the French don’t say “je veux” (I want): it sounds too blunt. They use “je voudrais” (I’d like) or “je prends” (I’ll have).
I’d like a coffee, please. (very polite)
I want ice cream! (what children say)
To call the waiter you say “S’il vous plaît !” or “Excusez-moi !”. Never “Garçon !”: it’s old-fashioned and rude.
In a restaurant: “la carte” = the list of all dishes; “le menu” = the set menu (entrée + plat + dessert at a fixed price); “le plat du jour” = the dish of the day.

Trap for English speakers: “l’entrée” = the FIRST course (the starter), while “le plat” = the main course. In American English “entrée” means the main course, so be careful. “Entrée” also means “entrance” to a building.
2. The partitive: du, de la, de l’, des
The partitive is new for English speakers. When you talk about an unspecified QUANTITY (some, any), French uses a special article. English often uses nothing: “I eat bread”, “I drink water”.
I’ll take a cheese (a whole one, a portion) → un
Golden rule: after aimer / adorer / détester → le, la, les. After manger / boire / prendre / acheter / il y a → du, de la, des.
As with “un, une”, after a negation the partitive becomes DE: “Je ne mange pas de viande”, “Je ne bois pas d’alcool”. That’s what Karim says in the dialogue.
3. Quantities: un verre de, une bouteille de
After a word showing quantity you only use DE (no article):
Just like English “a glass OF wine”. Don’t say “un verre du vin”.
Three basic irregular verbs for the restaurant. The singular forms all sound the same.
Conjugated like “prendre”: “apprendre” (to learn) and “comprendre” (to understand): “Je comprends” = “I understand”, “Je ne comprends pas” = “I don’t understand”. Very useful!
“Je voudrais” also comes from “vouloir”, but in the conditional (the polite form). For now, learn it as a set phrase.
A few things that surprise tourists:
Tap water is free in restaurants. This is how you ask for it.
Bread is always free and is put straight on the table, without a plate.
Service is included in the price. Tipping is optional (a few euros).
The bill doesn’t come by itself: you have to ask for it.
Before eating you say “Bon appétit !”, and when clinking glasses “Santé !” (Cheers!) or “Tchin-tchin !”.
After a quantity: just de / d’.
Je voudrais un café, s’il vous plaît.
I’d like a glass of red wine.
L’eau du robinet au restaurant est…
